summary: Return the index of any element strictly greater than its neighbours (out-of-range neighbours count as -infinity), in O(log n) time.
mainInsight: If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], walking right from mid either keeps rising until the last element (a peak, since nums[n] = -inf) or eventually turns down (a peak at the turn), so the right side must contain a peak; otherwise mid or something to its left is a peak. One comparison discards half the array even though it is not sorted.
invariant: The range [lo, hi] always contains at least one peak of the whole array; the loop stops when lo == hi, and that index is the peak.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.summary: Return the first i with nums[i] > nums[i + 1]; if none, return n - 1.
weaknesses: Violates the stated O(log n) requirement
approaches.interviewRelevance: Mention as the baseline, then move to binary search; the statement explicitly rules it out.

approaches.name: Binary search on the slope
approaches.summary: lo=0, hi=n-1; while lo < hi compare nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1]; move lo = mid + 1 on a rising slope, else hi = mid.
weaknesses: Less obvious: binary search on unsorted data needs the existence argument
approaches.interviewRelevance: The expected answer; the interviewer will ask why it works on an unsorted array.

commonMistakes: Thinking binary search needs a sorted array and giving up on O(log n).
Using `while lo <= hi` with `hi = mid` (infinite loop or IndexError on nums[mid + 1]).
Setting hi = mid - 1 on a falling slope, which can discard the peak at mid.
Comparing with nums[mid - 1] and reading index -1 (Python silently wraps to the last element).
edgeCases: Single element: index 0 is a peak.
Strictly increasing array: the last index is the peak.
Strictly decreasing array: index 0 is the peak.
Multiple peaks: any one is accepted.

cards.answer: Binary search on the slope, comparing nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1] and moving toward the larger neighbour. Clue: The statement demands logarithmic time, and with nums[-1] = nums[n] = -infinity and no equal neighbours, the rising side of any mid is guaranteed to contain a peak.

cards.explanation: The array is unsorted, but binary search only needs a test that tells you which half still holds an answer. Comparing mid with its right neighbour is that test: the uphill side must reach a peak because the boundary is -infinity. A linear scan works but ignores the explicit logarithmic-time requirement.

promptVariants: If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], why is a peak guaranteed somewhere to the right of mid?
Prove that moving toward the larger neighbour of mid can never miss every peak.
Why does the uphill side of mid always contain a peak?
cards.answer: Walk right from mid + 1. Either the values keep rising to the last element, which is a peak because nums[n] = -infinity, or they turn down at some index, and that turning point is larger than both neighbours. Equal neighbours are forbidden, so there is no flat stretch to get stuck on.
keyPoints: Keep rising -> last element is a peak (nums[n] = -inf)
Turn down -> the turning point is a peak
No equal neighbours, so no plateaus
cards.explanation: This existence argument is what licenses binary search on unsorted data: you do not need order, only a test that tells you which half is guaranteed to hold an answer.

promptVariants: What invariant do lo and hi maintain in the canonical loop?
State the loop invariant that makes `return lo` correct.
What is always true about the range [lo, hi] during the search?
cards.answer: [lo, hi] always contains a peak of the whole array. lo = mid + 1 keeps the rising side (which has a peak); hi = mid keeps mid itself, which may be the peak. The range strictly shrinks, and when lo == hi the single remaining index is a peak.
keyPoints: Both updates keep a peak inside
lo == hi -> that index is the peak
cards.explanation: Initially [0, n-1] holds a peak because the boundary is -infinity. Each update keeps the half that provably holds one, so the invariant survives until one index is left.

cards.answer: mid itself may be the peak, so it must stay in the range
cards.explanation: nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1] only proves mid beats its right neighbour; it may also beat its left one and be the peak. Dropping it can lose the only peak in the range, e.g. nums = [1, 3, 2].

promptVariants: What happens if `while lo < hi` is changed to `while lo <= hi` in this code? Try nums = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] and nums = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10].
Why does this loop use `lo < hi` instead of `lo <= hi`? Trace both inputs: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] and [2, 4, 6, 8, 10].
cards.code:
lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
while lo <= hi:  # changed from lo < hi
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]:
        lo = mid + 1
    else:
        hi = mid
return lo
cards.answer: When lo == hi the loop keeps going with mid == hi. On [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] the range reaches lo == hi == 0, the else branch sets hi = mid = 0 again, and it loops forever. On [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] it reaches lo == hi == 4 and nums[mid + 1] = nums[5] raises IndexError. `lo < hi` stops at one candidate, which by the invariant is the peak, and guarantees mid + 1 <= hi stays in range.
keyPoints: lo == hi with hi = mid never shrinks -> infinite loop
mid == n - 1 makes nums[mid + 1] out of range
lo < hi guarantees mid < hi, so mid + 1 is valid
cards.explanation: With hi = mid (not mid - 1) the loop must stop at a one-element range, since hi = mid cannot shrink it. That is also what keeps mid + 1 in range.

promptVariants: Derive the time complexity of this code.
What is the running time of this code, and which lines determine it?
cards.answer: O(log n). Each iteration sets lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid, so the range [lo, hi] roughly halves every time, and each iteration does O(1) work (one comparison). After about log2(n) iterations, lo == hi.
keyPoints: Range halves each iteration (lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid)
cards.explanation: Same halving argument as classic binary search; the only difference is the comparison (mid vs mid + 1 instead of mid vs target).

cards.answer: O(1): only lo, hi and mid are stored
cards.explanation: The loop is iterative and indexes into nums in place; three integers are all it keeps.

cards.explanation: The scan always finds a peak (the first descent, or the last index), but it runs in O(n). The statement explicitly requires O(log n), which only the slope binary search gives.
